doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Writing for Kai Winding's trombone group
summary: He wrote Nutcracker and The Preacher for Kai's group, which played jazz clubs and later dances, with Carl, Dick Lieb and Don Sebesky involved.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So you did some arranging for the trombone group with Kai. And how many trombones was that? © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Thanks to Bill Harris. Bill said, “Kai is going to do a record,” he says, “sit down and write an original piece of music.” And I did and it was the first original piece — not the first original piece, I shouldn’t say, I did some in the service, but I didn’t do a whole lot of original pieces. But I wrote this piece called, I named it “Nutcracker.” And I only named it “Nutcracker” — I don’t know what made me name it “Nutcracker.” Because Connecticut is the Nutmeg State I think, isn’t it? I think Connecticut is the Nutmeg State. And whether I had Connecticut on my mind or whether when I was writing this piece I thought this might be a ballbuster to play and I called it “Nutcracker,” I don’t really know why I called it “Nutcracker,” but I called it “Nutcracker” anyways. And Kai liked it. Recorded it on the first record. As a matter of fact he liked it so much that it was — when we’d finished doing the album, and I don’t have the videotape of this but I have the audiotape, we finished doing the album and before we went on the road we were on the Steve Allen Show, which was The Tonight Show then. And we did two tunes, “Nutcracker” and that thing we did with the [humms] from “Carousel” — “Little Girl” was it? The tune from “Carousel.” And we were — because Steve Allen made mention that we were going to this club in Philadelphia, back to this club in Philadelphia called Pep’s, where I had been with Woody Herman. It was an active club in Philadelphia in those days. And I did that and I did some more things. I think the things that I did that were recorded, I did “The Preacher” which was a simple arrangement. It wasn’t a copy of Horace Silver’s arrangement, but it certainly had Horace Silver’s inspiration behind it. But it wasn’t a copy of Horace Silver’s arrangement. Especially, there was a shout chorus and everything else that was totally different from Horace Silver’s arrangement. But I loved that record of Horace Silver’s, “The Preacher,” so I did that. And then I did some other things, I can’t quite remember what they were. But then we started playing jazz clubs pretty much exclusively. We’d go to a place and be there a week or two or something like that. We went to a place, Porky’s Hideaway in Florida and we were there for like a month just playing jazz music. And then — I don’t know if it was before Carl left or not but Kai decided that he wanted to make more money. So that’s when we decided, I started to do a lot of writing, Dick Lieb and myself, of just standard tunes. He wanted a lot of tunes, we were going to play dances. So there was just like any tune, I don’t know, and just harmonize it and then go on to another tune. It was no fancy arranging, it was just a tune. And I think Carl — Carl doesn’t like to stay with one thing too long anyways, no matter what it is, but I think Carl left around this time and that’s when Don Sebesky came on. And Don Sebesky came on the group, I remember it was in the summertime because Don was out of school. He went to the Manhattan School of Music and he came on the group for the summertime, and Don was the one that told me, he says, “Wayne,” he says, “you should go to school.
